## Answer

Write the form as a sum of squares of three linear forms. Their coefficient matrix is

$$M=\begin{pmatrix}1&1&0\\0&1&-1\\1&0&1\end{pmatrix}.$$

The quadratic-form matrix is $M^TM$, so its rank equals $\operatorname{rank}M$. Since the third row is the first minus the second and the first two rows are independent, $\operatorname{rank}M=2$. Therefore the rank of the quadratic form is $\boxed{2}$.

## Answer

Over the real numbers, $\operatorname{rank}(AA^T)=\operatorname{rank}A$. Thus the stated rank is two exactly when all $3\times3$ minors of the displayed $3\times4$ matrix vanish while its rank remains two. The four maximal minors factor as

$$2(a-2),\quad 2(a-2)(a+1),\quad (a-2)(a+2),\quad (a-2)(a+6).$$

They vanish simultaneously only for $a=2$, and direct substitution gives rank two. Hence $\boxed{a=2}$.

Let

$$L=\begin{pmatrix}1&0&0\\1&1&0\\1&1&1\end{pmatrix},\qquad B=\operatorname{diag}(a_1,a_2,a_3).$$

The displayed matrix satisfies $A=LBL^T$. Therefore choosing $C=L^{-T}$ gives $C^TAC=B$. Explicitly,

$$\boxed{C=\begin{pmatrix}1&-1&0\\0&1&-1\\0&0&1\end{pmatrix}}.$$

## Answer

For

$$A=\begin{pmatrix}3&2&1\\2&2&1\\1&1&1\end{pmatrix},\qquad D=\operatorname{diag}(2,3,1),$$

one convenient congruence factor is

$$C=\begin{pmatrix}\sqrt6/3&-\sqrt2&0\\0&3\sqrt2/2&-\sqrt2/2\\0&0&\sqrt2\end{pmatrix}.$$

It is upper triangular with nonzero diagonal, so it is invertible. Direct multiplication gives

$$\boxed{C^TAC=D}.$$

## Answer

The quadratic-form matrix is

$$A=\begin{pmatrix}1&-2&2\\-2&4&-4\\2&-4&4\end{pmatrix}=vv^T,\qquad v=(1,-2,2)^T.$$

Thus its eigenvalues are $9,0,0$. Choose the orthonormal eigenvectors

$$q_1=\frac13(1,-2,2)^T,\quad q_2=\frac1{\sqrt5}(2,1,0)^T,\quad q_3=\frac1{3\sqrt5}(-2,4,5)^T.$$

For $Q=(q_1,q_2,q_3)$ and $x=Qy$,

$$Q^TAQ=\operatorname{diag}(9,0,0),\qquad \boxed{f=9y_1^2}.$$

## Answer

The quadratic-form matrix is

$$A=\begin{pmatrix}2&0&0\\0&3&a\\0&a&3\end{pmatrix}.$$

Its eigenvalues are $2,3-a,3+a$. Matching the given standard-form coefficients $1,2,5$ and using $a>0$ gives $\boxed{a=2}$. Unit eigenvectors for $1,2,5$ are respectively

$$q_1=\frac1{\sqrt2}(0,1,-1)^T,\quad q_2=(1,0,0)^T,\quad q_3=\frac1{\sqrt2}(0,1,1)^T.$$

Thus $Q=(q_1,q_2,q_3)$ is the required orthogonal transformation matrix and $Q^TAQ=\operatorname{diag}(1,2,5)$.

## Answer

The matrix of the quadratic form is

$$A=\begin{pmatrix}1&\alpha&1\\\alpha&1&\beta\\1&\beta&1\end{pmatrix}.$$

The given standard form has eigenvalues $0,1,2$, hence characteristic polynomial $\lambda^3-3\lambda^2+2\lambda$. Direct calculation gives

$$\det(\lambda I-A)=\lambda^3-3\lambda^2+(2-\alpha^2-\beta^2)\lambda+(\alpha-\beta)^2.$$

Comparing coefficients yields $\alpha^2+\beta^2=0$ and $\alpha=\beta$. Over the reals this gives

$$\boxed{\alpha=0,\ \beta=0}.$$

## Answer

The matrix expression is

$$f=x^TAx,\qquad A=\begin{pmatrix}0&2&-2\\2&4&4\\-2&4&-3\end{pmatrix}.$$

Its eigenvalues are $-6,1,6$, with mutually orthogonal eigenvectors $(1,-1,2)^T$, $(-2,0,1)^T$, and $(1,5,2)^T$. Hence take

$$Q=\begin{pmatrix}1/\sqrt6&-2/\sqrt5&1/\sqrt{30}\\-1/\sqrt6&0&5/\sqrt{30}\\2/\sqrt6&1/\sqrt5&2/\sqrt{30}\end{pmatrix}.$$

Then $Q^TAQ=\operatorname{diag}(-6,1,6)$, so under $x=Qy$ the standard form is

$$\boxed{f=-6y_1^2+y_2^2+6y_3^2}.$$

## Answer

The matrix has diagonal entries $a$ and every off-diagonal entry equal to $2$. Its eigenvalues are

$$a+4 \quad(\text{for }(1,1,1)^T),\qquad a-2 \quad(\text{with multiplicity two}).$$

The standard form $6y_1^2$ has eigenvalues $6,0,0$. Therefore $a-2=0$ and $a+4=6$, giving $\boxed{a=2}$.

## Answer

The matrix is

$$A=\begin{pmatrix}a&0&b\\0&2&0\\b&0&-2\end{pmatrix}.$$

Its trace is $a$, so $a=1$. Its determinant is $-4-2b^2=-12$, and $b>0$, hence $\boxed{b=2}$. The eigenvalues are $2,2,-3$. Choose

$$q_1=(0,1,0)^T,\quad q_2=\frac1{\sqrt5}(2,0,1)^T,\quad q_3=\frac1{\sqrt5}(1,0,-2)^T.$$

With $Q=(q_1,q_2,q_3)$,

$$Q^TAQ=\operatorname{diag}(2,2,-3),$$

so $x=Qy$ gives $\boxed{f=2y_1^2+2y_2^2-3y_3^2}$.

## Answer

Since every row sum is $3$, $(1,1,1)^T$ is an eigenvector with eigenvalue $3$. The matrix has rank one, so its other two eigenvalues are zero. Therefore an orthogonal transformation reduces the quadratic form to

$$\boxed{f=3y_1^2}$$

(up to a permutation of the new coordinates).

## Answer

Because $\operatorname{rank}(A^TA)=\operatorname{rank}A$, all $3\times3$ minors of the displayed $4\times3$ matrix must vanish. Each contains the factor $a+1$, and the condition gives $\boxed{a=-1}$. Then

$$A^TA=\begin{pmatrix}2&0&2\\0&2&2\\2&2&4\end{pmatrix}.$$

Its eigenvalues are $0,2,6$, with unit eigenvectors

$$q_1=\frac1{\sqrt3}(-1,-1,1)^T,\quad q_2=\frac1{\sqrt2}(-1,1,0)^T,\quad q_3=\frac1{\sqrt6}(1,1,2)^T.$$

Thus for $Q=(q_1,q_2,q_3)$ and $x=Qy$,

$$\boxed{f=2y_2^2+6y_3^2}.$$

## Answer

Since $\alpha^Tx=a_1x_1+a_2x_2+a_3x_3$ and similarly for $\beta$,

$$f=2(\alpha^Tx)^2+(\beta^Tx)^2=x^T(2\alpha\alpha^T+\beta\beta^T)x.$$

Hence the matrix is $\boxed{2\alpha\alpha^T+\beta\beta^T}$. If $\alpha,\beta$ are orthogonal unit vectors, extend them to an orthonormal basis $(\alpha,\beta,\gamma)$. For $Q=(\alpha,\beta,\gamma)$,

$$Q^T(2\alpha\alpha^T+\beta\beta^T)Q=\operatorname{diag}(2,1,0),$$

so the standard form is $\boxed{2y_1^2+y_2^2}$.

## Answer

Relative to the orthonormal basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$, the coefficients are $(2,1,-1)$. The new basis is $(e_1,-e_3,e_2)$, so the coefficients are reordered to $(2,-1,1)$; changing the sign of an eigenvector does not change its eigenvalue. Thus the new standard form is

$$\boxed{2y_1^2-y_2^2+y_3^2},$$

which is $\boxed{(A)}$.

## Answer

The quadratic-form matrix is

$$A=\begin{pmatrix}2&1&-4\\1&-1&1\\-4&1&a\end{pmatrix}.$$

The standard form has rank two, so $\det A=-3(a-2)=0$, giving $\boxed{a=2}$. The eigenvalues are $-3,6,0$, with mutually orthogonal eigenvectors $(1,-1,1)^T$, $(-1,0,1)^T$, and $(1,2,1)^T$. Thus one valid orthogonal matrix is

$$Q=\begin{pmatrix}1/\sqrt3&-1/\sqrt2&1/\sqrt6\\-1/\sqrt3&0&2/\sqrt6\\1/\sqrt3&1/\sqrt2&1/\sqrt6\end{pmatrix},$$

and $Q^TAQ=\operatorname{diag}(-3,6,0)$. Hence $\lambda_1=-3,\lambda_2=6$ (their order may be exchanged).

## Answer

Orthogonal congruence preserves the eigenvalues. The standard form has diagonal entries $1,-2,3$, so

$$\det A=1\cdot(-2)\cdot3=-6,\qquad \operatorname{tr}A=1-2+3=2.$$

Therefore the answer is $\boxed{(-6,2)}$, namely $\boxed{(C)}$.
